strengths: The combination of low-resolution drafting, learned token up/down-sampling, and spatially expanded local correction is a meaningful contribution to accelerating next-token image generators without retraining the target model. It exploits image structure beyond conventional token-level speculative decoding.

Table 1 demonstrates useful improvements over the implemented speculative baselines. At 1024p, MuLo-SD achieves 1.68× decoding speedup versus LANTERN’s 1.42×, with higher GenEval accuracy (76.3 versus 75.4). Relative to standard Tar decoding, its GenEval and DPG-Bench reductions are modest: 0.8 and 0.3 points.

The evaluation covers two resolutions, complementary semantic and perceptual metrics, qualitative comparisons, and threshold sweeps. Figure 5(c) provides particularly useful evidence that expanding rejected neighborhoods improves the speed–alignment tradeoff over isolated local correction in the relevant operating range.

The supplementary material provides substantial implementation information, including training losses, optimizer settings, model sizes, sampling parameters, and latency breakdowns. It also candidly reports weaker baseline drafter accuracy and quality degradation at aggressive acceleration settings.
weaknesses: The experiments do not isolate the central multi-scale contribution. Figure 5 ablates sampler losses, pooling, and rejection strategies, but does not compare against a single-scale drafter using the same threshold-based acceptance and local expansion. Consequently, the gains over LANTERN cannot be attributed specifically to multi-scale drafting rather than the substantially different verification rule.

Practical advantage over existing image acceleration remains unestablished. At 1024p, training-free ZipAR achieves 3.65× speedup versus 1.68× while also obtaining better values on all four reported quality metrics. A contribution need not beat the strongest baseline, but calling the approaches orthogonal does not demonstrate complementary value; their proposed combination is untested.

The end-to-end acceleration claim is overstated. Section 6 explicitly excludes approximately 17 seconds of conditioning generation, despite Section 4.2 describing nearly 70% faster end-to-end generation and Figure 7 labeling latency as E2E. Using the supplied timings, including conditioning reduces the speedups to approximately 1.10× at 512p and 1.50× at 1024p, before other pipeline costs.

The acceptance mechanism needs a clearer technical specification. Equation (5) pools over B_k, whereas Algorithm 1 uses the TVD-constrained A_{k,δ}. Threshold acceptance and retaining later tokens after changing their prefix do not inherit standard speculative sampling’s distribution-preservation guarantee or automatically inherit LANTERN’s bound. Approximate generation is a valid objective, but the manuscript does not characterize the resulting error, and the implementation description does not explain how affected KV-cache entries are refreshed during local resampling.

Evidence for quality preservation and generality is limited. All results use one model family, the 1024p setting lacks component ablations, and no uncertainty estimates accompany small metric differences. At 1024p, MuLo-SD worsens FID from 32.4 to 32.8 and HPSv2 from 29.5 to 28.4; LANTERN obtains FID 31.1 at its reported operating point. Thus the improvement is principally a speed–semantic-alignment tradeoff, rather than uniform superiority. Overall, the original design and demonstrated decoding gains place this near the acceptance boundary, but incomplete contribution isolation and unresolved technical specification prevent a stronger recommendation.

strengths: The combination of low-resolution drafting, learned token up/down-sampling, and spatially expanded local correction is a plausible contribution to accelerating next-token image generation without retraining the target model.

Evaluation covers two resolutions, two semantic-alignment benchmarks, perceptual metrics, and qualitative examples. The threshold sweeps expose the speed–quality tradeoff rather than reporting only one favorable operating point.

Figure 5 provides meaningful evidence for local neighborhood expansion, particularly around 1–1.5× speedup. The supplement also provides training settings, sampling parameters, neighborhood-radius experiments, and a latency breakdown.
weaknesses: The evidence does not adequately isolate the central multi-scale contribution. The ablations vary sampler losses, probability pooling, and rejection neighborhoods, but do not compare against a same-resolution drafter using the same threshold and local-expansion rule. Consequently, the improvements over LANTERN cannot be attributed specifically to multi-scale drafting rather than the substantially different acceptance and correction procedure.

The demonstrated practical advantage is limited. In Table 1, training-free ZipAR achieves 1.88× versus 1.22× speedup at 512p and 3.65× versus 1.68× at 1024p, while also achieving better reported quality metrics. Beating the strongest baseline is not necessary for acceptance, but calling ZipAR orthogonal does not demonstrate an additional benefit: the proposed combination is untested, and MuLo-SD requires trained samplers and another resolution-specific model.

The main text overstates end-to-end acceleration. Section 6 explicitly excludes approximately 17 seconds of MLLM conditioning from latency measurements. Using the reported approximate decoding times, full-pipeline speedups are about 1.10× at 512p and 1.50× at 1024p, rather than 1.22× and 1.68×. This materially changes the claimed user-facing benefit.

The acceptance procedure is heuristic and its approximation is insufficiently characterized. Equation (5) replaces rejection sampling with a probability threshold, and accepted downstream tokens remain accepted after earlier context changes. LANTERN’s distributional bound does not establish a bound for this procedure. Exact sampling is not required for a useful method, but claims of preserving quality should be qualified: Table 1 shows degradation relative to Tar in every reported quality metric, and Figure 13 illustrates increasing artifacts as acceptance is relaxed.

Important implementation details remain ambiguous. Equation (5) pools over B_k, whereas Algorithm 1 uses A_{k,δ}; the algorithm also scales token counts by r despite defining r as the spatial resolution ratio, which implies r² scaling. Cache recomputation after noncontiguous corrections is not explained, although it affects both conditional correctness and runtime. These issues extend beyond cosmetic notation and hinder faithful reproduction.

Overall, the supported local-correction insight and measured speculative-baseline improvements are worthwhile, but the missing attribution experiment, overstated end-to-end benefit, and unresolved implementation details leave the current balance in favor of weak rejection. The single-model evaluation is a limitation, not independently a reason to reject.

strengths: The combination of low-resolution drafting, learned token up/down-sampling, and spatially expanded local rejection is a meaningful contribution to accelerating next-token image generators without retraining the target model. It adapts useful image-specific structure to speculative generation.

Table 1 supports improved speed–alignment trade-offs over the implemented speculative baselines. At 1024p, MuLo-SD achieves 1.68× speedup and 76.3 GenEval, versus LANTERN’s 1.42× and 75.4; at 512p, it achieves 1.22× versus 1.08× with nearly identical GenEval.

Evaluation covers two resolutions, two semantic-alignment benchmarks, and complementary perceptual metrics. The supplementary threshold sweeps and qualitative examples help expose the speed–quality trade-off rather than reporting only one favorable operating point.

The local-expansion mechanism has useful empirical support: Figure 5(c) shows better GenEval at moderate speedups than either raster-scan rejection or local rejection without expansion. The supplement also provides radius ablations, training settings, baseline-adaptation details, and latency breakdowns.
weaknesses: The practical advantage remains uncertain because the training-free ZipAR baseline substantially outperforms MuLo-SD in the same setting. At 1024p, ZipAR achieves 3.65× speedup with 76.6 GenEval, 32.4 FID, and 29.6 HPSv2, versus 1.68×, 76.3, 32.8, and 28.4 for MuLo-SD. Calling the methods orthogonal does not establish an additional benefit, and their combination is not evaluated. This does not invalidate the proposed idea, but materially limits the demonstrated usefulness.

The end-to-end acceleration claim is overstated. Section 6 explicitly excludes approximately 17 seconds of MLLM conditioning from latency measurements, whereas Section 4.2 describes nearly 70% faster end-to-end generation. Using the supplied approximate timings, the 1024p full-pipeline speedup is about (17 + 80)/(17 + 80/1.68) = 1.50×; at 512p it is about 1.10×. The measured component acceleration is real, but its scope should be reported consistently.

The verification procedure is a heuristic whose distributional behavior is insufficiently characterized. Equation (5) replaces rejection sampling with a probability threshold, and accepted tokens can remain after their conditioning prefix changes during resampling. LANTERN’s TVD constraint therefore does not establish a bound for the complete MuLo-SD sampler. Exactness is not necessary for this contribution, but claims of preserving quality need qualification: Table 1 shows reduced HPSv2 at both resolutions, and Figure 13 shows increasing distortion at permissive thresholds.

The experiments do not isolate the benefit of multi-scale drafting from the changed verification rule: there is no comparable single-scale drafter using the same threshold and local expansion. Moreover, all results use one model family, and the explanation that LANTERN performs worse because Tar is stronger remains a hypothesis. These limitations narrow the support for general superiority over image speculative-decoding methods.

Some reproducibility details are internally inconsistent. Equation (5) pools over B_k, while Algorithm 1 uses A_{k,δ}; the algorithm divides token counts by r despite defining r as a spatial ratio, for which sequence lengths scale by r². Handling target KV-cache states after scattered token corrections is also insufficiently explained. These are correctable specification issues, but affect faithful reproduction.

strengths: The paper proposes a useful combination of low-resolution drafting, high-resolution verification, and spatially localized correction for accelerating existing next-token image generators. This introduces a coarse-to-fine inference strategy without retraining the target model for next-scale prediction.

The strongest results demonstrate a meaningful speed–quality trade-off. On Tar-7B at 1024p, Table 1 reports 5.33× decoding acceleration, with GenEval changing from 85.2 to 85.4, DPG-Bench from 80.4 to 80.8, and FID improving from 37.9 to 34.8, although HPSv2 decreases. These results support practical value beyond merely matching a benchmark leader.

Evaluation covers two model families, two Tar model sizes, two output resolutions, and complementary semantic and perceptual metrics. The training-free pixel-space upsampling variant improves applicability, while the supplement provides useful sampling settings, training details, and latency breakdowns.

Figure 5 provides substantive component analysis: neighborhood expansion improves the speed–alignment trade-off over isolated local rejection, and parallel drafting/resampling substantially improves efficiency. The paper also acknowledges the memory cost of maintaining two checkpoints and sensitivity to alignment between resolutions.
weaknesses: The headline end-to-end acceleration is overstated. Supplement Section 6 explicitly excludes approximately 17 seconds needed to generate Tar’s conditioning sequence, while Section 4.3 claims 4–5× faster end-to-end generation. Using the reported 80-second 1024p decoding baseline and 3.90× Tar-1.5B decoding speedup gives approximately (17 + 80)/(17 + 80/3.90) = 2.59× for the combined stages. The decoding gains remain valuable, but the distinction materially affects practical usefulness.

The evidence does not establish consistently superior trade-offs over ZipAR. On LlamaGen, MULO-SD achieves 1.40× versus ZipAR’s 1.88×, with worse GenEval and DPG-Bench but better FID. On Tar-1.5B at 512p, 1.94× versus 1.88× comes with lower scores on all four quality metrics. At 1024p, Tar-1.5B gains only about 7% in decoding throughput over ZipAR while HPSv2 falls from 29.6 to 28.7. The stronger Tar-7B result is compelling, but broad claims of consistent dominance are unsupported.

Important details of the approximate verification and resampling procedure remain ambiguous. Equation 5 pools over B_k, whereas Algorithm 1 uses the TVD-constrained A_{k,δ}; these can produce different acceptance decisions. Resampling earlier tokens also changes the context used to verify retained later tokens. Spatial locality motivates this approximation, but does not establish conditional independence or transfer LANTERN’s distributional bound. The manuscript does not adequately specify attention masking, stale KV-cache handling, or conditioning on unresolved tokens during concurrent island resampling, limiting reproducibility of the central acceleration mechanism.

The experiments do not fully isolate the contribution beyond existing parallel decoding. Figure 5(d) compares the combined method against its sequential version, but there is no matched comparison separating parallel low-resolution drafting, parallelism across islands, and ZipAR within islands. An upsample-only baseline is also absent, leaving the amount of quality recovered by target-model verification unclear. These omissions matter because the strongest gains depend on the combined pipeline.

Uncertainty and resource reporting are insufficient to interpret the smaller gains: no repeated-run variability or confidence intervals accompany the small semantic-score differences, and peak memory is not measured despite the additional checkpoint and caches. There are also correctable table errors—for example, Tar-1.5B at 1024p changes FID from 32.4 to 31.3, but labels this +0.4. Overall, the useful high-resolution results and coherent design place the paper near acceptance, while the latency framing, incomplete algorithm specification, and uncertain incremental advantage keep the recommendation borderline.

strengths: The combination of low-resolution drafting, spatially expanded rejection, and parallel resampling is a meaningful contribution to accelerating next-token image generators without retraining the target model. The default pixel-space upsampler also avoids training a dedicated drafter.

The strongest result is substantial: on Tar-7B at 1024p, Table 1 reports 5.33× decoding acceleration versus ZipAR’s 3.65×, with slightly higher GenEval and DPG-Bench scores and improved FID relative to the unaccelerated model. This supports practical value despite the accompanying HPSv2 reduction.

Evaluation includes two model families, multiple resolutions, semantic and perceptual metrics, and relevant baselines. Figure 5 supports the importance of neighborhood expansion and parallel decoding; the supplementary threshold sweeps and latency breakdown provide useful additional evidence.
weaknesses: The central end-to-end acceleration claim is overstated. Supplementary Section 6 explicitly excludes approximately 17 seconds of conditioning generation. Using its approximate 80-second 1024p decoding baseline, the reported 3.90× Tar-1.5B acceleration corresponds to about (17+80)/(17+80/3.90) = 2.59× for the combined pipeline, before other overheads. This materially changes the practical interpretation of the headline result.

The claim of consistently outperforming competing methods is not supported. On LlamaGen, MULO-SD reaches 1.40× versus 1.59× for LANTERN and 1.88× for ZipAR, with worse semantic scores. On Tar-1.5B at 512p, its advantage over ZipAR is only 1.94× versus 1.88× while all four quality metrics are worse. At 1024p, Tar-7B shows a convincing speed advantage, but HPSv2 falls from 30.5 to 29.5. The evidence supports a setting-dependent tradeoff rather than general superiority.

The operative verification rule is ambiguous: Equation 5 pools over B_k, whereas Algorithm 1 uses the TVD-constrained A_{k,δ}, and the supplement specifies δ=0.1. These are different acceptance rules. Moreover, threshold acceptance and retaining tokens after earlier context changes do not inherit standard speculative decoding’s distribution-preservation guarantee. Approximate sampling is reasonable here, but the actual rule and scope of distributional control need clearer specification.

The parallel algorithm underlying the strongest results is insufficiently specified. Algorithm 1 describes sequential resampling, while Section 3.4 introduces concurrent rejection islands without detailing attention masks, conditioning on unresolved preceding islands, or KV-cache updates after earlier tokens change. These choices affect both output quality and measured efficiency, making this a substantive reproducibility concern.

Experimental attribution remains incomplete. Figure 5 establishes benefits within the proposed pipeline, but there is no direct low-resolution generation plus super-resolution baseline to isolate the value of target verification, and ZipAR is evaluated at one setting rather than with a comparable speed–quality sweep. No uncertainty estimates establish whether the small semantic-score differences are meaningful.

Several reporting errors need correction: for Tar-1.5B at 1024p, FID 31.3 versus 32.4 is annotated as +0.4, and HPSv2 28.7 versus 29.5 as -0.3. Algorithm 1 also uses r rather than r² for token-count scaling despite defining r as the spatial resolution ratio. These are individually correctable, but compound uncertainty about the reported configuration. Overall, the useful high-resolution results place the paper near the acceptance boundary, while latency scope and algorithmic reproducibility prevent a clear acceptance recommendation.

strengths: The combination of low-resolution drafting, high-resolution verification, and spatially expanded local resampling is a useful contribution to accelerating next-token image generators. It exploits image structure without retraining the target model, and the default pixel-space upsampler requires no additional training.

Table 1 supports meaningful acceleration with largely preserved semantic alignment. At 1024p, Tar-7B achieves 5.33× decoding speedup, versus ZipAR’s 3.65×, while GenEval changes from 85.2 to 85.4 and DPG-Bench from 80.4 to 80.8. Tar-1.5B achieves 3.90× with small semantic-score decreases.

Evaluation includes two Tar sizes, LlamaGen, two output resolutions, semantic and perceptual metrics, and qualitative comparisons. Figures 5 and 9 provide useful evidence that neighborhood expansion improves the speed–quality tradeoff and that parallel decoding substantially strengthens the method.

On balance, the supported high-resolution acceleration and practical integration provide a stronger case for acceptance. The contribution remains valuable despite uneven advantages across models and the qualifications below.
weaknesses: The claim of 4–5× faster end-to-end generation is overstated. Supplementary Section 6 explicitly excludes approximately 17 seconds of MLLM conditioning generation. Using its approximately 80-second 1024p decoding baseline, Tar-1.5B’s 3.90× decoding speedup corresponds to roughly 2.59× for conditioning plus decoding. This materially changes the user-facing efficiency claim.

The method does not consistently outperform the strongest baseline. On LlamaGen, it achieves 1.40× versus ZipAR’s 1.88× and LANTERN’s 1.59×, with lower semantic scores. On Tar-1.5B at 1024p, its advantage over ZipAR is modest, while HPSv2 falls to 28.7 versus 29.6. The results support a useful operating-point tradeoff rather than universal superiority or unchanged perceptual quality.

The verification procedure is heuristic: Equation 5 omits the proposal-probability correction, and accepted tokens can retain decisions computed under prefixes later changed by resampling. Spatially disconnected islands are also not necessarily independent under causal attention. Exact sampling is not required for this contribution, but the manuscript should distinguish its empirical quality preservation from the distributional guarantees discussed for conventional speculative decoding and LANTERN.

Reproducibility of the strongest parallel variant is incomplete. Algorithm 1 describes sequential resampling rather than island-wise parallel execution; attention masking and KV-cache handling after context changes are insufficiently specified. Equation 5 pools over B_k, whereas Algorithm 1 uses A_{k,δ}; the algorithm also uses linear sequence-length scaling by r despite the stated r² spatial expansion.

Some reported differences need more cautious interpretation. No uncertainty estimates accompany small metric gains, and Table 1 contains incorrect deltas: Tar-1.5B at 1024p changes FID from 32.4 to 31.3, not +0.4, and HPSv2 from 29.5 to 28.7, not −0.3. These are correctable reporting flaws, distinct from the substantive efficiency and algorithm-specification concerns.
